lessons.title: Why You're Not Growing on Instagram (Easy Fixes)
objectives: Diagnose a stalled account from its own numbers
Fix the causes in the order that pays
Tell a content problem apart from a positioning problem
lessons.notes:
Accounts stall for a small number of reasons, and the numbers tell you which one before you change anything.

WORK THROUGH IT IN THIS ORDER.

ARE PEOPLE SEEING IT AT ALL? If reach is low on everything, the problem is the content, not the account. There is no shadowban to blame - almost every claim of one turns out to be content nobody watched.

DO THEY WATCH PAST THE FIRST SECONDS? If the drop is right at the start, it is a hook problem, and Module 3 fixes it.

DO THEY WATCH TO THE END? If they leave in the middle, the video is too long, too slow, or answers the question later than it should. Cut the preamble and get to it.

DO THEY SHARE OR SAVE IT? If they watch and do nothing, the content is pleasant but not useful. Nobody sends a pleasant video to a friend. Teach something, name something, or be funny enough to be worth passing on.

DO THEY FOLLOW AFTER WATCHING? If a video reached fifty thousand people and gained eleven followers, the video worked and the profile did not. Look at the bio and the grid a stranger lands on.

IS IT THE SAME PEOPLE EVERY TIME? Reach confined to existing followers means the content is not travelling, and that is a hook and shape problem, not a posting-time problem.

WHAT IS ALMOST NEVER THE REASON: the time of day, the number of hashtags, and the platform being against you. These absorb enormous attention because they are easy to change.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - two local diagnoses that standard lists miss. First, POSTING TOO BROADLY. An account trying to speak to everyone in the world reaches nobody in particular, while one that is clearly about a single town, trade or community gets picked up locally and becomes sellable to local businesses. Narrower is faster here. Second, INCONSISTENCY CAUSED BY COST AND TIME rather than laziness - if data and daylight are the real constraint, the fix is batching a fortnight of filming into one good session, not resolving to post daily.
lessons.practice: Take your last fifteen posts and write down four numbers for each: reach, percentage still watching at three seconds, percentage watched to the end, and shares. Find which of the six steps your account fails at first. Fix only that one for the next two weeks and compare the same four numbers.

quiz.question: A video reached 50,000 people and gained eleven followers. What is wrong?
options: The profile - the video worked but the profile did not convert the visitors
The hook
The posting time
The hashtags

quiz.question: People watch to the end and then do nothing. What does that mean?
options: The content is pleasant but not useful enough to share or save
The video is too long
The hook is weak
The account is shadowbanned

lessons.title: How To Go Viral on TikTok Every Time You Post
objectives: Separate what is repeatable from what is luck
Build the conditions that make a hit more likely
Convert a spike into something that lasts
lessons.notes:
Take the title as marketing. Nobody goes viral every time, including the people who teach it, and a course that pretended otherwise would be lying to you. What IS repeatable is raising your chances and being ready when it happens.

WHAT ACTUALLY RAISES THE ODDS:
VOLUME WITH JUDGEMENT. More attempts, each one reviewed. Ten considered videos beat a hundred careless ones and beat one perfect one.
A SUBJECT THAT TRAVELS. Something people recognise, argue about, or need. Too narrow limits the ceiling; too broad wins nothing.
A HOOK THAT EARNS THE SECOND. Non-negotiable.
A SHAPE PEOPLE FINISH. Short, looping, no dead air.
SOMETHING WORTH SENDING. Shares are the multiplier, so make something a person would forward to one specific friend.

WHAT DOES NOT: posting at a magic hour, hashtag formulas, buying views, deleting and reposting, and engagement pods. All widely sold, and none of them survive contact with the numbers.

THE PART NOBODY PREPARES FOR IS THE SPIKE. A video takes off, fifty thousand strangers arrive, and the account has nothing for them - a bio that says nothing, no pinned post, no way to buy, no next video. The spike passes in three days and leaves almost nothing behind. BEFORE it happens: fix the bio, pin your best work, give them somewhere to go, and have the next videos ready. WHEN it happens: post again quickly on the same subject, read the comments because they are the source of your next twenty videos, and do not change what you make.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - be clear about what a spike is worth here. Views alone pay nothing, because platform payout programmes are largely unavailable in Kenya. A hundred thousand views is worth exactly what you convert it into: followers who will see your next post, people on WhatsApp who buy, a brand that gets in touch, or a portfolio piece that wins you a client. So decide the conversion BEFORE you post - what should someone do after watching - and make sure the bio lets them do it, because working that out afterwards is how people end up with a big number and no income.
lessons.practice: Before posting anything else, get ready for a spike: rewrite the bio, pin your three best posts, set one clear next step, and film three videos to hold in reserve. Then write down, for your next ten posts, what you want a viewer to do after watching, and check that the profile actually lets them do it.

quiz.question: What is the honest reading of going viral every time you post?
options: Nobody does it; what is repeatable is raising the odds and being ready for the spike
It is achievable with the right posting schedule
It works only for large accounts
It requires paid promotion

quiz.question: What is a hundred thousand views worth to a creator here?
options: Exactly what you convert it into, since platform payouts are largely unavailable
A fixed amount per thousand views
Nothing at all, in every case
Automatic brand sponsorship

lessons.title: Editing a Viral-Style Reel in CapCut, Start to Finish
objectives: Edit a finished short video on a phone
Use cuts, captions and sound to hold attention
Build a repeatable edit instead of starting fresh each time
lessons.notes:
CapCut is free, runs on a phone, and does everything a short video needs. This lesson is the practical edit.

THE ORDER THAT SAVES TIME: cut first, then captions, then sound, then the cover. People do it backwards, caption a rough cut, then re-cut and have to redo every caption.

CUTTING. Remove every pause, every breath before a sentence, and every word before the first useful one. The first frame should already be the hook. A short video has no room for anyone settling in, including you.

PACE. A change roughly every two to three seconds - a cut, a zoom, a new image on screen - because a static talking head loses people even when the words are good. Do not make it frantic; make it never still.

CAPTIONS. Auto-generate, then read every line and fix it. Names, places and local words come out wrong every time, and a wrong caption is what viewers notice. Keep the text away from the edges, where the interface covers it.

SOUND. Music under speech, quiet enough that the words win. Where there is no speech the sound carries the whole video, and choosing one already circulating helps.

THE LOOP. Make the last frame run naturally into the first. A clean loop earns rewatches, and rewatches are the strongest multiplier available.

EXPORT at the highest setting the phone allows, and upload on wifi where you can.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - build a TEMPLATE and stop starting from nothing. Save one project with your caption style, font, position and sizing already set, then duplicate it for every video. That turns a forty-minute edit into ten, and it is the actual difference between people who sustain posting and people who stop. Watch storage and export size, because a full phone and a heavy upload on a bundle are the two things that quietly end a posting habit. And keep the edit honest for a client - never cut a before-and-after so it shows a result the work did not produce, because that is the reputation you are building, and here it travels by word of mouth.
lessons.practice: Edit one video end to end in the order given - cut, caption, sound, cover - and time yourself. Then save that project as your template with the caption style already set, and edit a second video from it. Write both times down; the second should take less than half the first.

quiz.question: What is the right order to edit in?
options: Cut, then captions, then sound, then the cover
Captions, then cut, then sound
Sound, then cut, then captions
Cover, then captions, then cut

quiz.question: Why build a saved template?
options: It turns a forty-minute edit into ten, which is what makes posting sustainable
It improves export quality
The platform ranks templated videos higher
It reduces phone storage use

lessons.title: Planning 30 Days of Content in One Sitting
objectives: Produce a month of content decisions in a single session
Batch filming and editing so posting does not depend on daily inspiration
Keep a plan that survives a week when nothing goes right
lessons.notes:
The reason accounts die is not that people run out of ideas. It is that deciding what to post, filming it and editing it all happen on the same day, so one busy day breaks the chain and the chain never restarts.

THE SITTING, in order.
1. PILLARS - your three or four subjects from Module 2.
2. THIRTY LINES - one line per post, spread across the pillars. Not scripts, a line each. Pull them from questions customers actually ask, from comments, from things you explained to someone last week, and from your own posts that already worked.
3. MARK THE SHAPE for each: transformation, how-to, mistake, list, behind-the-scenes, story, answer.
4. GROUP BY WHAT THEY NEED - everything filmed at the shop together, everything to camera together, every screen recording together.
5. FILM IN TWO SESSIONS, not thirty. Same light, same setup, change the shirt where it matters.
6. EDIT IN BATCHES from your template.
7. QUEUE OR SCHEDULE, so the posting day needs no decision at all.

REPEAT WHAT WORKED. A post that did well can be remade in a different shape, updated, or simply posted again months later. Almost nobody saw it the first time, and this is the cheapest content you will ever make.

LEAVE GAPS DELIBERATELY. Four or five slots a month for whatever is actually happening - a trend, a question, a busy week. A plan with no gaps is abandoned the first time life interferes.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the version that fits a real week here. Batch around DAYLIGHT AND DATA: one Saturday morning of good light produces a fortnight, and uploading a batch on wifi saves real money against posting daily on a bundle. Keep the plan in a notebook or a phone note rather than a paid tool, because the tool is not the point and the subscription is another foreign-currency bill. And plan around what actually happens locally - school terms, end of month when people have been paid, harvest, Ramadan, December - because content landing when people have money and attention does more than the same content in the third week of January.
lessons.practice: Sit down once and produce thirty lines across your pillars, each marked with its shape and grouped by what it needs to film. Book two filming sessions in daylight, leave five slots empty for the month, and mark which weeks fall at end of month or a school term. Film the first batch before the week is out.

quiz.question: Why do accounts actually die?
options: Deciding, filming and editing all happen on the same day, so one busy day breaks the chain
The creators run out of ideas
The platform stops showing older accounts
Followers lose interest over time

quiz.question: Why leave slots in the plan empty?
options: A plan with no gaps is abandoned the first time life interferes
The platform penalises full schedules
It reduces data costs
It leaves room for paid promotion

lessons.title: 35 Places to Find Clients as a Freelance Social Media Manager
objectives: Find the first paying clients for short-form video work
Lead with a specific service rather than a general offer
Approach a business in a way that actually gets a reply here
lessons.notes:
You have a specific skill now - making short video that gets reach - and that is a narrower and better-paid offer than general social media management. Sell that.

WHERE THE CLIENTS ACTUALLY ARE, in order of how likely a beginner is to close them:
BUSINESSES YOU ALREADY BUY FROM. The salon, the gym, the butchery, the hardware, the restaurant. You know the product, you are a real customer, and you can walk in.
BUSINESSES WITH A DEAD ACCOUNT. One last posted to eleven months ago is a business that tried and could not sustain it. That is your opening, not a closed door.
BUSINESSES ALREADY ADVERTISING. Anyone paying for ads has a budget and already accepts paying for marketing.
PEOPLE YOU KNOW who run something, and their contacts. The first three clients almost always come from here.
LOCAL BUSINESS GROUPS on WhatsApp and Facebook, where being the person who answers questions usefully is worth more than posting an advert.
EXISTING CLIENTS, ASKED. The easiest new client is a referral from a satisfied one, and nobody asks.
ONLINE FREELANCE PLATFORMS, which are crowded and priced low, but are somewhere to collect early reviews.

WHAT TO SHOW. You do not need clients in order to have a portfolio. Make three videos for a real local business without being asked, make them well, and show them. This works more often than any message, because it is the work instead of a claim about the work.

HOW TO APPROACH: specific, short and about them. What you noticed, what you would do, what it would cost. Not a paragraph about your passion for digital marketing.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - what actually gets a reply here. WHATSAPP, NOT EMAIL. Business email goes unread; WhatsApp is where business is done, and a short voice note is normal and often answered faster than text. WALKING IN WORKS, particularly outside Nairobi, and it beats every online method for a first client - go at a quiet hour, ask for the owner, show the three videos on your phone. Have an answer ready for the price question, as a small clear first package rather than a monthly retainer, because a business that has never paid for this will not begin with a commitment. And take a deposit before you film, agreed in writing on WhatsApp, because chasing the balance afterwards is the commonest way freelancers here lose money.
lessons.practice: List twenty businesses you personally buy from and check which have a dead or weak account. Choose three, film and edit one good video each without being asked, and take them to the owner in person or on WhatsApp with a short specific note and one clear price. Write down how many replied and what they asked.

quiz.question: What works better than a message claiming you can help?
options: Three good videos already made for that business, shown to the owner
A detailed written proposal
A price lower than competitors
A portfolio of foreign brands

quiz.question: What is the commonest way freelancers here lose money?
options: Filming before taking a deposit, then chasing the balance
Charging too little for the first job
Working without a contract template
Taking on too many clients at once

lessons.title: What to Charge as a Social Media Manager
objectives: Price short-form video work for this market without underselling
Choose a package shape a small business will actually buy
Set the terms that get you paid
lessons.notes:
Pricing is where most beginners here lose money, usually by charging for their time as though it were worth nothing and then resenting the client.

PRICE THE OUTPUT, NOT THE HOURS. A client buys a number of finished videos a month, not your afternoon. Hourly pricing punishes you for getting faster, and getting faster is exactly what happens.

COUNT EVERYTHING before naming a number: planning, travel, filming, editing, captions, writing, posting, replying to comments, the messages from the client, revisions, and the report. Beginners count the editing only, quote for that, and discover the job is four times what they priced.

PACKAGE SHAPES THAT SELL HERE:
A SMALL FIRST PACKAGE - a set number of videos, one filming session, one month. Defined, affordable, and it lets a business that has never paid for this try you without committing.
A MONTHLY RETAINER, once the first package has worked. State exactly what is included: how many videos, how many filming sessions, how many revisions, and what is not included.
A ONE-OFF PRODUCTION DAY for a business that only wants the content and will post it themselves. Often the easiest sale of the three.

SET A FLOOR - what you need to earn in a month divided by how many clients you can genuinely serve well - and do not quote below it. Work taken below your floor is done badly or resentfully, and it also becomes the price you are known for.

RAISE IT AS THE WORK IMPROVES. Your first client price is not your permanent price; new clients get the new rate.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the terms that decide whether you are actually paid. TAKE FIFTY PER CENT BEFORE YOU FILM and the balance before the videos are handed over, on M-Pesa, with the amounts and the scope written into the WhatsApp thread, because that thread is your contract and it has settled arguments. STATE THE REVISION LIMIT in writing, since unlimited revisions is how a fair price becomes a bad one. Charge the filming session separately when the client is far, because travel and a day gone are real costs. Quote any advertising budget as the client's separate cost, never inside your fee. And say so honestly when a business does not need a retainer - some need one good production day and to be taught to post it themselves - because that is what wins you the referral that follows.
lessons.practice: Write out every task in one month of work for one client and estimate the hours honestly, including messages and revisions. Calculate your monthly floor. Then write three offers - a small first package, a production day, and a monthly retainer - each stating what is included, the revision limit and the payment terms.

quiz.question: Why price the output rather than the hours?
options: A client buys finished videos, and hourly pricing punishes you for getting faster
Hours are harder to keep track of
Clients prefer larger numbers
Output pricing is required by the platforms

quiz.question: What stops a fair price becoming a bad one?
options: A revision limit stated in writing
A larger deposit
A longer contract period
Charging separately for travel
